Roughly alright when it's a look at the hardships of poverty, largely because it's willing to exist in a matter-of-fact realism unencumbered by any real sense of style beyond simply that of observing spaces with undistinguished flatness, which is not a diss, it's a legitimate aim for a story like this, and it allows for the believable, lived-in nature of Smith's performance and its settings to further the emotional understanding of these economic hardships and how hard it really is to be poor. Pretty awful whenever it ventures into a feel-good story of a random guy just impressing the cool stockbrokers and hanging around with them and being elevated because he's that cool and that good and that much of a #Grinder, which idea is also the central principle of the entire film--Chris Gardner is a real Sigma American Worker, the guy who was left behind by his Bitch Wife, but he did it, he grinded and grinded and grinded and grinded and ultimately he Got It Made, and it's cool because those rich Wall Street guys really are nice and wonderful and lovable, sure, maybe they don't understand quite what it's like not to be rich and that some people don't always need to do what they want, but hey--he did it! Any actual interest this has in poverty is undone by the film's ultimate veneration of the American Dream, the myth of making it in this perfect, nice little world if you just work hard enough, all just set-dressing for feel-good inspirational pablum ultimately less invested in any of the injustices and tragedies it presents than in the possibility to transform their tragic and unjust nature into elements of an essentially nice, perfect, wonderful world. The whimsical music in the beginning drives the point home, none of the sadness really means too much, and the ending's disinterest in Gardner's future past "making it" only makes its existence as more of a middle-class pablum more obvious--poverty and its horrors are reimagined as the inspirational starting point of a true American Dream, and if Gardner made it, so could you, and there's no need to really think of much else. The world is perfect and the lesser parts of it are both unfixable and of import only in how they help improve images of a good life. This is not a triumph; this is a tragedy. For every Chris Gardner there are thousands of unnamed casulties ground beneath the wheels of an unjust system—a system designed to desecrate, dehumanize, and destroy. The Pursuit of Happyness was made in dedication to the featureless tyranny of American capital. A film produced and funded by the very same empty suits that are responsible for letting this sort of horror story happen in the first place. Cannibalistic little mutants wrapped in Super 150's wool, patting your back with one hand while picking your pocket with the other. Greedy fingers stretching, straining, reaching. They'll take everything they can find—your wallet, your keys, your dignity—and then plunge their hands deep into your gut to pull out your entrails. You'll collapse right there in the street while they pick through your belongings. Even though their ill-gotten gains may be stained red with your lifeblood, it's not like they care; their machines will launder it all until it's squeaky clean and smelling of lavender. And just like that, the last known traces of your existence will be erased from this world, washed away under a torrent of past-due bills and foreclosure notices. You'll disappear. The strange, awful men at the top of the financial food chain will have already forgotten about you; their atrophied brains too dumb to do anything besides make them smile their too-wide smiles. They'll lie there in their eight thousand dollar designer chairs and rub their swollen stomachs, their teeth bloody and dripping. Their gullets will pulse with the still-beating hearts of their prey—just some of the many, many delectable sweetmeats that are prepared specially for them by their employees, the very same employees that hope against hope that they never find themselves ending up on those silver platters once the clock strikes twelve. Those monsters are the only ones that truly pursue happiness in America. They love this movie—every scene, every tiny little detail. And of course they would love it, since they were the ones who made it. They used their great, big machines to shape it, forming the thing out of primordial clay until it could walk, then run, and finally leap into movie theaters all across the globe. Their cinematic construct said whatever they wanted it to, parroting an endless torrent of lies designed to sell us on a system that does not work and will never work. Sure, Mr. Gardner had very real struggles, but he overcame those issues by joining the ranks of the new bourgeois. His reward for enduring those hardships? He gets to schmooze with the sorts of people who would've crossed to the other side of the street if they saw his younger self coming. He gets to run interference for them, making their inhumanity palatable to the general public. And he gets an invitation to their ghoulish feasts, where he can crack open the bones of the dishonored dead and suck out the marrow of their existence. I doubt it tastes very good.

The Pursuit of Happyness the first time I watched this movie was in a theater, about four years ago. Hanane had invited me, and honestly, at the time, it was kind of rough: we were bored out of our minds. 😭 I definitely didn’t think that, a few years later, this would become a movie I’d find so deeply moving. It’s an extremely emotional, sentimental, and deeply human film. But what makes it even more heartbreaking is knowing that it’s inspired by the true story of Chris Gardner. Everything you watch takes on a different meaning when you realize that his struggles, failures, sacrifices, and moments of complete desperation actually happened. It isn’t simply a fictional story designed to make us emotional  this really happened to someone. And knowing that makes it hurt so much more. I absolutely loved the originality and the way the story is constructed. We follow a man going through a period where it seems like everything is constantly working against him, yet he keeps moving forward. Chris Gardner isn’t portrayed as someone who simply gets lucky and suddenly becomes successful. He works, he perseveres, he gets rejected, he experiences homelessness and poverty, but he refuses to give up, especially because of his son. And that’s probably what I took away from the movie the most: good deeds, sacrifices, hard work, and perseverance eventually pay off. His success doesn’t happen overnight, nor does it feel like some convenient miracle. It comes after countless struggles, closed doors, humiliations, and moments when giving up would have been the easiest thing to do. The relationship between Chris and his son is also beautiful. The movie isn’t simply about achieving professional success; it’s about a father desperately trying to build a better life for his child while barely managing to survive himself. Some of their scenes are incredibly simple, but that simplicity is precisely what makes them so powerful. There’s also this idea running through the entire movie: you can lose almost everything without losing your determination to keep going. Chris Gardner is constantly confronted with adversity, but he never completely lets go of the belief that another life is possible. So yeah, I genuinely think it’s a beautiful film. Not only because it’s emotional, but because its message, as universal as it may be, remains incredibly powerful: success doesn’t erase the hardships you went through; sometimes, it gives them meaning.

| Tier 2/5 — Mixed | The Pursuit of Happyness isn’t a bad film. It’s somewhat emotionally effective, Will Smith gives a strong performance, and the relationship between Chris and his son has enough genuine warmth to carry a lot of the movie. There are moments that work exactly as intended, and I understand why people find it inspiring. My problem with it is that the film is constantly brushing against something much more complicated and interesting, then retreating into the safest possible version of its story. The clearest example is Chris insisting on keeping his son with him after his wife leaves. Linda has a job opportunity and family connections, while Chris is entering an unpaid internship with no guarantee of employment and is already in an incredibly unstable financial position. Yet the film basically asks us to accept that keeping his son with him is automatically the noble choice because Chris loves him and wants to be a present father. Eventually they are homeless and sleeping on a bathroom floor together, and the movie presents this almost entirely as evidence of Chris’s devotion and perseverance. That is an incredibly strange situation when you actually look at it without the inspirational framing. Chris would rather have his child experience homelessness with him than temporarily stay with his mother, who has work and a support system. There is clearly pride involved in that decision. There is also possessiveness and perhaps a need for Chris to prove to himself that he is the better parent. None of that means he doesn’t love his son. In fact, that contradiction is exactly what could have made him such an interesting character: a genuinely loving father whose determination starts becoming selfishness, and who may be forcing his child to suffer because he cannot separate being a good father from refusing to let go. But the custody issue isn’t really my biggest problem with the film by itself. It is more like a perfect miniature of what I think is wrong with the movie as a whole. Whenever the story arrives at something morally uncomfortable, it simplifies it. Chris’s pride becomes determination. His reckless decisions become courage. Linda’s completely understandable desire for stability is barely explored because giving her too much legitimacy would complicate the film’s heroic image of Chris. Even the son’s suffering is mostly treated as another obstacle Chris has to overcome rather than something that might make us question his choices. The fact that Chris eventually succeeds makes this even easier for the film. Because he gets the job, everything that came before is retrospectively treated as if it must have been justified. His gamble worked, so the movie never really has to ask whether it was responsible. Success becomes moral vindication. But if he had been one of the nineteen interns who didn’t get hired, exactly the same decisions would suddenly look much less heroic. The outcome doesn’t actually change the morality of putting a child through that kind of instability, but the film behaves as though it does. I also don’t think the film is particularly well shot. It isn’t ugly or incompetent, but visually it feels anonymous. The filmmaking mostly illustrates whatever emotion the scene already wants us to feel: handheld tension during stressful moments, softer intimacy between father and son, grim surroundings during poverty, and the expected emotional emphasis during scenes like the bathroom sequence. The bathroom scene works because the situation is devastating and Smith sells it, not because the visual direction is doing anything especially revealing. That visual conventionality connects to the same larger problem. The camera almost never challenges Chris or gives us another way of looking at him. It doesn’t create much distance between the audience and his own understanding of what he is doing. A more interesting film might have made that bathroom floor feel not only tragic but unsettling. It could have forced us to notice that there is a small child here paying the price for an adult’s gamble. Instead, the filmmaking keeps directing our sympathy toward Chris’s suffering and away from the possibility that he has helped create some of it. That is ultimately why the film frustrates me despite the fact that I still think it works. It has the material for a much richer character study about ambition, masculinity, pride, parenthood and the point where admirable persistence becomes destructive obsession. Instead, it mostly settles for an inspirational story about refusing to give up. There is nothing inherently wrong with that story, and the film tells it competently. I just think the more uncomfortable version sitting underneath it is far more interesting. The bathroom floor is basically the entire movie in miniature. If you completely accept Chris’s view of himself, it is a heartbreaking image of a father refusing to abandon his son while fighting through impossible circumstances. If you question that perspective even slightly, it becomes something much more troubling: a father holding his sleeping child on a public bathroom floor partly because his own pride would not allow him to choose the safer option. The film only really wants to explore the first interpretation. I wish it had been brave enough to confront the second.

I have a lot of mixed feelings on this one. It has some moments that were sweet. The acting was great. I've actually seen this before and remembered liking it quite a bit. But this time, I struggled a bit. Largely because I never actually really liked Chris Gardner. Everything he was doing felt really selfish. He demanded his kid stay with him even though he knows he has no way to support his kid. And as a result him and his kid have to really struggle. And it's kind of all his fault. He has another option by allowing the kid to go with his mom to New York. So the movie just made me feel frustrated and kind of pissed off at Chris that he couldn't put his own ego aside to just do what's best for his kid. Now it didn't really make sense to me that the mom didn't fight harder. I just felt like I was missing part of the story. Turns out I was and quite a bit. In the true story, Chris cheated on his wife and got his mistress pregnant. She tried to take their son but he kind of assaulted her and was arrested for that. She does end to taking their kid to New York deciding not to press charges and then eventually ends to taking the kid back after a few months to live with his dad. Then after he becomes a broker he arranged for the kid to stay with her due to his long work hours. This feels like important info to leave out. Finding this out, it just feels like the movie wasn't honest with me. And I find that to be kind of gross to be honest. If I were to treat this as a fictional story, I might feel a bit different. Still didn't like Chris Gardner, but I at least would respect that he was at least able to eventually future things out. And that itself can be a inspirational story. So the story isn't a bad one. But I am mixed on the message. In the ending, while Will Smith is narrating, he says this moment of my life is called happiness. And I don't know how I feel about that. Because having a successful career is not equivalent to happiness. Happiness can be found without success in your career. I do get that if you have no money or resources at all, and your basic human needs aren't being met, it is going to be hard to actually be happy. But having a lot of money isn't really what makes one happy. And it just feels like this movie unintentionally sends the message that to be happy you need to find success in your career, and I don't really think that's true. The Pursuit of Happyness ist der American Dream Film schlechthin. Man muss nur alles geben, hart arbeiten und daran glauben, dann wird der Erfolg schon kommen. Nun, natürlich ist da etwas dran, egal, wie man ansonsten zu diesem Denken steht. Das Problem dieses Films liegt für mich nicht in der Geschichte, die er erzählt, denn die ist nett gemeint und zusätzlich mit toller Musik unterlegt. Doch es wird vorausgesetzt, dass wir diesen Erfolg selbst miterleben. Dass wir am Ende mindestens so aufgeregt sind wie Chris, ob er den Job nun bekommt oder nicht. Es muss das Publikum emotional mitreißen. Und hier komme ich zu meinem Hauptproblem des Films: Das schafft er einfach nicht. Jedenfalls nicht bei mir. Aber man möge mir die Möglichkeit geben, mich zu erklären. Uns werden mehrere Situationen geschildert, die Chris immer wieder den Boden unter den Füßen wegziehen. Die Ehefrau verlässt ihren Mann und ihr Kind. Die Gläubiger stehen förmlich vor der Tür. Man verliert die Wohnung. Alles Situationen, in die man nicht gelangen möchte, da sie potenziell die eigene Existenz, beziehungsweise die der Familie bedrohen. Und während uns all das geschildert und gezeigt wird, geht The Pursuit of Happyness auf die wichtigsten Fragen, die sich aus dieser Konsequenz ergeben, nicht ein. Denn, was macht all das mit den Menschen? Was macht es mit einem, ständig unsicher zu sein, was als Nächstes passiert? Und wie reagiert man darauf? Diese Fragen ergeben sich gezwungenermaßen aus der Handlung. Doch darüber erfährt man kaum etwas. Dafür sind die Dialoge/ das Drehbuch insgesamt zu oberflächlich. Es werden hier und da schöne Worte gefunden, um die Botschaft des Films zu formulieren(was in den Szenen auch sinnvoll ist, nicht nur Exposition, was der Film aussagen möchte). Aber das Innere der Charaktere wird so gut wie gar nicht beleuchtet. Dadurch verliert der Film enorm viel an Gewicht, weil die emotionalen Szenen dann natürlich nicht so stark wirken können, wie sie sollten. Hinzu kommt, dass The Pursuit of Happyness quasi durchgängig optimistisch ist. Was ich auch per se nicht schlecht finde, allerdings war es dem Film in diesem Fall meiner Ansicht nach nicht zuträglich. Das passiert hauptsächlich durch die Musik und Kamera, die beide wirklich gut sind, aber ich hätte mir gewünscht, manchmal auch etwas kälter in der Inszenierung zu sein, da man dadurch eher Mitgefühl erzeugt hätte. Somit ist tolle Kameraarbeit, tolle Musik, gutes Schauspiel und eine eigentlich motivierende Botschaft in einem zu oberflächlichen Film gefangen und kann seine Wirkung nicht so wirklich entfalten.

Shockingly, this film came out before the late-00s financial crisis. It would have felt even more relevant a year or two later, when a LOT of people were feeling a money crunch. But its concerns are sadly evergreen. Times are really tough right now, and I feel that as a parent of three kids. When the film focuses on that, it’s very effective. I want to see a struggling father succeed for the sake of his son, of course. I am quite privileged, but I think about what I would do to provide for my family if the worst happened. The film loses me in the details, though. It feels like Chris is in this mess because of many boneheaded decisions made before and during the film that strain my sympathies. His wife leaves and he insists that she’s incapable of caring for their son. Why? I’ve seen no indication that she’s a poor mother. Am I supposed to read that as Chris’ pride or his understanding that his wife is a poor provider? And his big win is becoming a stockbroker, the kind of person who creates financial crises that will put more people in these conditions. A lot of these thoughts are front-loaded in the film for me. The ending pulls at the heartstrings just right and makes me feel the joy. But I found it a slog to get there. All that aside, the big takeaway here is Will Smith. It’s a great acting performance, it’s a better box office performance. Smith was the biggest movie star of the 00s. Whether it was action, sci-fi, a rom-com, an original superhero film, his films were successful. He could take this schmaltzy, manipulative pap and make it one of the top ten films of the year. His star power was off the charts, and that’s rewlly interesting to me. Watched as part of a 20th anniversary 2006 retrospective.
As Paige said “it was like watching someone have a bad day for 2hr.” The emotion was great, I was invested, but the only emotion was struggle for literally the whole film. Too much running.

It’s well made for the most part, and it boasts career best performances from both Will and Jaden Smith (not that that’s saying much in Jaden’s case, but I digress). The message of this movie is essentially that you can work yourself out of poverty by working hard enough and being treated poorly by rich white guys. I understand that this is based on a true story, and that Chris Gardner actually did manage to work hard enough to get out of the dumps, but this movie isn’t interested in engaging with the class system that it relies on to get dramatic moments out of. Film del 2006, diretto da Gabriele Muccino. Chris Gardner viene lasciato dalla moglie e si ritrova ad affrontare enormi problemi economici, dovendo al tempo stesso prendersi cura del figlio piccolo Christopher. Questo film drammatico mi colpisce sempre molto personalmente. Nonostante presenti qualche limite dal punto di vista tecnico, la sceneggiatura, ispirata a eventi realmente accaduti, riesce sempre a coinvolgermi emotivamente. Narra la storia di un uomo che ha scommesso sull’investimento sbagliato e che si ritrova a dover far fronte a una serie di disavventure che si intrecciano con gravi problemi economici. Dallo sfratto all’abbandono da parte della moglie, passando per lo scarso profitto dei macchinari che cerca invano di vendere, Chris arriva a decidere di cambiare vita, trovando il coraggio e l’ambizione di intraprendere una nuova strada: uno stage non retribuito come broker. È commovente la dedizione, la passione e la resilienza di Chris, il quale, nonostante i numerosi problemi, continua imperterrito sulla propria strada, cercando di barcamenarsi tra il lavoro come venditore, la gestione del figlio e l’impegno dello stage, che prevede ore di studio ma anche l’acquisizione di nuovi clienti. Questo film ci ricorda quanto, anche nei momenti più bui, spesso ci si possa aggrappare a qualcosa, cercando di cambiare l’ordine degli addendi e, di conseguenza, il risultato della propria vita. Il coraggio di Chris, la sua abnegazione conciliata all’ambizione, hanno come propulsore principale la sofferenza, la povertà e l’incapacità di dare al proprio figlio ciò che desidera. E forse questo film, ripeto, nonostante presenti qualche pecca tecnica, mi colpisce sempre nel profondo, probabilmente proprio per le tematiche affrontate, che coincidono con un particolare periodo della mia vita. Questo lungometraggio, per quanto mi riguarda, è terapeutico: un film che, a ogni visione mi migliora l’umore e mi fa credere un po’ di più in me stesso. Per quanto concerne il comparto tecnico, la regia di Muccino prevede un utilizzo della macchina a mano che reputo disordinato e poco pulito. L’angolazione con cui viene posta la macchina da presa in alcune scene non mi convince, così come non mi convince appieno il blocking degli attori, in particolar modo nelle scene domestiche o in quelle racchiuse entro quattro mura. Risultano invece più azzeccate le scene all’aperto, ambientate in una New York movimentata, con Chris che inizialmente sembra andare quasi sempre nel verso opposto rispetto alla folla. Il film, invece, si conclude con un Chris perfettamente integrato in quella stessa folla, mentre cammina sui marciapiedi di New York. Gradisco questa rappresentazione di una New York frenetica e caotica. La macchina da presa si concentra spesso sulle lunghe file nei dormitori della Caritas, fotografando una parte della popolazione in difficoltà. Apprezzo l’intenzione di Muccino di mostrare anche questo volto della città, lontano dall’immagine patinata e idealizzata di New York. Will Smith è ottimo e riesce a essere estremamente coinvolgente dal punto di vista emotivo. Ottima anche la performance del giovane Jaden Smith. Voto: 8

A Classic American Dream Movie, But A Tone Deaf Film First I want to say I actually don’t dislike this film. I thought it was a good fun watch that was obviously made with lots of care and good intentions. The low lows we experience with Chris are trully devastating making it feel like your really there struggling alongside him. The amount of time and care the producers put into Chris’s personality and life make you really feel for him and see that he doesn’t deserve to be in this terrible situation. It has everything you would want in an American Dream™️ Movie. The zero to hero story, idealizing capitalism, and the ultimate message of work hard and you can achieve anything. But that’s not true. And this brings me to my main problem with this film. The Ideal (Fake) America Chris, the rest of his family and all the other characters, live in an ideal America free of racial or class bias that does not exist and has Never existed. This film focuses on the struggle of the working class black man in 1980s America but forgets about the fact he is working class and more importantly black. You really expect the audience to believe that in 1981 a rich millionaire CEO is inviting a black middle class intern with him to a football game in his private box because he just knocked on his door. Chris faces no sort of pressure or discrimination in this regard. Changing his race would have zero impact on the story. It seems Chris himself doesn’t even know he’s black. He is constantly quoting Thomas Jefferson a known racist and proud slave owner, and watching Ronald Reagan on the tv (No idea what that scene added). The film also glamorizes Chris bringing his son with him into homeless because he’s “In the pursuit of happiness” and it’s all gonna work out. While simultaneously shaming his wife for wanting to take her son away to a better place Final Notes It’s still a good movie overall aside from all these complaints. Will smith did a great job as Chris and Jayden was phenomenal. To think he was only around 7 years old when this was filmed is insane.
